lead: A blockchain has no server in the middle. Every computer running the software is a peer, equal to the others, and peers find each other on their own. Together they form an overlay network: a logical mesh of TCP connections laid over the ordinary internet. This chapter covers the three architectures, the join-and-discover procedure, the gossip that spreads each new transaction, and the security measures that keep an open network usable. Bitcoin and Ethereum run on exactly this design.
prereq: You need: nodes and network structure from Unit 1 (Blockchain networks and nodes), and hash pointers from Unit 2 (Linking blocks with hash pointers).

blocks.text: A node is any computer running the blockchain software. A peer is that node seen from the outside, as an equal partner rather than a servant. The pattern of connections among peers is the overlay network: a logical graph drawn on top of the physical internet. We draw the graph; the wires underneath are TCP connections.

Client-server. One central server holds the data and clients ask it. Cheap and fast, but the server is a single point of failure and a single point of control. A bank's account database behind UPI is close to this shape.
Pure peer-to-peer. Every node is both client and server. No node is privileged, and any node may leave without stopping the network. Gnutella in 2000 was the first large pure design.

Hybrid. A few nodes take extra jobs: supernodes relay more traffic, bootstrap servers only hand out addresses. Bitcoin is pure at run time but hybrid at start-up, because a brand-new node needs one first address from somewhere.

Short history. Napster (1999) kept a central index and moved only the files peer-to-peer. Gnutella removed the index and flooded queries. BitTorrent (2001) cut files into pieces and used a central tracker to find holders; later versions replaced the tracker with a DHT. Bitcoin (2009) was the first P2P network carrying money, so its peers must also agree on one order of transactions — see Consensus mechanisms and their types.

sections.h3: Joining the network and spreading data

items: Read the seed list: a few IP addresses hardcoded in the source code, plus DNS seed hostnames. Resolving a DNS seed returns a batch of live peer addresses.
Open a TCP connection to one or two of those addresses.
Handshake: each side sends a version message (protocol version, services, timestamp, own address, best chain height); each replies verack. Both sides now know whom they are talking to.
Ask for more addresses with getaddr. Peers reply with addr messages, each carrying several (IP, port, services, timestamp) entries. The node saves them in an address book and drops stale ones.
Dial the new addresses, grow to a target number of connections, and repeat as peers come and go.

Gossip: a new transaction is passed to every connected peer, and each of them passes it onward. Duplicate detection stops it being passed on again; designs that flood, such as Gnutella, also add a hop limit.

blocks.text: Structured lookup. In a distributed hash table (DHT), every node and every key hash into the same identifier space. Each node keeps a small set of contacts at every distance from itself — a few near neighbours and a few far ones. A lookup for key k jumps to a contact closer to k each hop, halving the remaining distance, so it needs about log₂ n hops for n nodes. Ethereum's discovery protocol uses a Kademlia-style DHT; Bitcoin uses the address-book gossip described above.

sections.h3: Unstructured, structured and hybrid overlays, and keeping the network safe

blocks.text: Unstructured overlay: no rule maps data to a particular node, so a message is flooded to neighbours with a hop limit called TTL (time-to-live), counted in hops. Gnutella works this way. The hop limit plus duplicate detection bound the work; the cost is that many peers receive the same message.

Bitcoin relays by announce-and-request. A node sends a small inventory hash (inv message) to its peers. A peer that does not already have the transaction replies with getdata, and the full transaction is then sent. Each node keeps a record of what it has already seen and stays silent about it afterwards. So peers exchange many small announcements rather than pushing the full transaction to everyone.

Structured overlay uses a DHT key, so a lookup goes almost straight to the right node. It is efficient and is used mainly for finding peers. Hybrid overlay, in this section's sense, uses a structured DHT for lookups and unstructured flooding for broadcast. Note that this is a different sense of 'hybrid' from Section 1, where it meant a few nodes carrying extra jobs.

items: Encrypted, authenticated transport: Ethereum's connection layer encrypts and authenticates every link, and Bitcoin offers an encrypted transport option, so a relay cannot read or quietly rewrite traffic.
Signatures: transactions and blocks are signed, so a relaying peer cannot alter them; the receiver validates before forwarding.
Peer scoring and banning: invalid data, a bad proof of work or a flood of messages earns a bad score, then a disconnect and a ban.
Connection diversity against an eclipse attack: many outgoing connections, address buckets split by IP range, and saved anchor peers, so one attacker cannot surround a node with its own peers.
Limits: maximum message size, hop count and message rate per peer, so one peer cannot exhaust memory or bandwidth.

blocks.text: Bitcoin and Ethereum are the standard examples. One line worth remembering: P2P crypto exchanges and P2P marketplaces are trading venues, not network topologies. A P2P exchange matches two users directly; an OTC exchange has a dealer quote a price; neither changes how nodes connect.

figure.caption: Each hop multiplies the copies by the fan-out of 3: 3, then 9, then 27. The hop limit stops the 27 peers holding the last round, so peers send 39 copies in all, and 40 copies exist once the originator's own copy is counted.

spec.title: Flooding with fan-out 3, TTL 3 hops
spec.aria: A chain of four steps: the originator sends 3 copies, those 3 send 9 more for a running total of 12, those 9 send 27 more for a running total of 39, and at TTL 0 the last 27 stop, leaving 40 copies counting the originator's own.

examples.question: A blockchain network floods each new transaction with fan-out 3 (each peer forwards to 3 neighbours that have not yet seen it) and time-to-live 3 hops. Count the copies sent in each round, the total copies sent by all peers, and the total counting the originator's own copy.
steps: Round 0, hop 1: the originator sends 3 copies. Copies sent so far = 3.
Round 1, hop 2: each of the 3 receivers forwards to 3 peers, so 3 × 3 = 9 copies. Running total = 3 + 9 = 12.
Round 2, hop 3: each of the 9 receivers forwards to 3 peers, so 9 × 3 = 27 copies. Running total = 12 + 27 = 39.
TTL is now 0, so the 27 receivers stop forwarding. Copies in the last round = 27.
The originator's own copy is never sent to anyone, so copies that exist = 39 + 1 = 40.
Duplicate detection applies: a peer that already holds the transaction does not forward it again, so the real count stays near 39 and does not explode.
examples.answer: All nodes together send 39 copies (the originator's 3 plus 9 plus 27), 27 of them in the last round; counting the original copy the originator still holds, 40 copies exist.
examples.check:
fan = 3
ttl = 3
total = 0
copies = 1
last = 0
for hop in range(ttl):
    copies = copies * fan
    total = total + copies
    last = copies
print(total)
print(last)
print(total + 1)

traps: Calling a P2P crypto exchange or a P2P marketplace a P2P network. Those are trading venues; the topology is unchanged.
Assuming a connected peer is a trusted peer. Any node may connect and may lie; every message is validated locally.
Calling Bitcoin fully pure P2P without noting its hardcoded seeds and DNS seeds at start-up — it is hybrid only during bootstrap.
Confusing a bootstrap node (hands out addresses, then steps aside) with a supernode (relays data for others).
Forgetting that flooding needs both a TTL and duplicate detection, and then claiming every node receives every message without limit.

quiz.q: Define node, peer and overlay network in one line each.
quiz.a: A node is a computer running the blockchain software. A peer is that node viewed as an equal partner in the network. The overlay network is the logical graph of connections among peers, built on top of ordinary internet links.

quiz.q: Name the two bootstrap aids a new Bitcoin node uses to find its first peers.
quiz.a: Hardcoded seed IP addresses in the source code, and DNS seed hostnames that resolve to lists of live peer addresses.

quiz.q: Why is Bitcoin called hybrid at start-up but pure at run time?
quiz.a: A new node has no addresses, so it asks a DNS seed or a hardcoded seed for a few peers — that is a helper role, so hybrid. Once connected, the node learns more addresses by getaddr/addr gossip and talks to equal peers only; no node stays privileged, so it is pure.

quiz.q: Flooding with fan-out 4 and TTL 2 hops. How many copies are sent per round, how many in total by peers, and how many exist counting the originator's copy?
quiz.a: Round 0: 4 copies. Round 1: 4 × 4 = 16 copies. Peers send 4 + 16 = 20 copies, with 16 in the last round. Adding the originator's own copy gives 21.

quiz.q: A Kademlia-style DHT holds 1,00,000 nodes. Roughly how many hops does one lookup take?
quiz.a: About log₂ n = log₂ 100000 ≈ 16.6, so about 17 hops, since 2¹⁷ = 131072 covers the network.

quiz.q: How does an eclipse attack work, and why do diverse outgoing connections and IP bucketing defeat it?
quiz.a: The attacker fills the victim's address book with addresses it controls, so all connections lead to the attacker, who can then hide blocks or feed a false chain. Diversity helps because the node dials many peers chosen from different IP ranges and keeps anchor peers, so the attacker cannot own every slot; any honest peer breaks the eclipse.

quiz.q: Why does gossip flooding need both a time-to-live and duplicate detection?
quiz.a: Without a TTL, a message would circulate forever in cycles. Without duplicate detection, the same transaction would be forwarded many times over and traffic would grow with the number of paths. Together they bound the work while still reaching nearly every node.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production, peer-to-peer networking is handled by libraries rather than hand-written code: libp2p (used by IPFS and Filecoin) and devp2p (Ethereum) package discovery, transport encryption and gossip. Ethereum's newer discovery, discv5, runs over UDP with topic-based routing. Hyperledger Fabric uses a gossip service to spread blocks among organisations in a permissioned network. Current research measures eclipse and Sybil resistance, peer diversity and block propagation delay; search 'eclipse attack Bitcoin', 'Kademlia DHT' or 'libp2p gossipsub' to go further.
